extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) involved in claim drafting and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and evaluation of patent claim language under 35 U.S.C. 112 (primarily second paragraph and sixth paragraph), covering Markush/grouping, negative limitations, multiplicity, product-by-process, means-plus-function, and related claim-drafting and examination issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush group propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: The materials set forth in the Markush group ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or to an art-recognized class. When the Markush group occurs in a claim reciting a process or a combination (not a single compound), it is sufficient if the members of the group are disclosed in the specification to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship, and it is clear from their very nature or from the prior art that all of them possess this property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double inclusion of an element by members of a Markush group is not, in itself, sufficient basis for objection or rejection — facts of each case must be evaluated to determine indefiniteness. The mere fact that a compound may be embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not necessarily render claim scope unclear (example: 'selected from the group consisting of amino, halogen, nitro, chloro and alkyl' acceptable even though 'halogen' is generic to 'chloro'). Where a Markush expression is applied only to a portion of a chemical compound, propriety is determined by considering the compound as a whole. Alternative phrasings ('selected from the group consisting of A, B, C and D' vs 'R is A, B, C or D') are acceptable if the grouping is proper. See MPEP § 803 and § 715.03 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenus / Genus claim acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus, subgenus, and Markush-type claims, if properly supported by the disclosure, are all acceptable ways for applicants to claim their inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not reject Markush-type claims merely because there are genus claims that encompass them. See MPEP § 608.01(p) and § 715.03. See also restriction practice in MPEP § 803.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Or" terminology acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative expressions using 'or' are acceptable, such as 'wherein R is A, B, C, or D.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases such as 'made entirely or in part of', 'at least one piece', and 'iron, steel or any other magnetic material' were held acceptable and not in violation of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (In re Gaubert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'optionally' in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'optionally' can be acceptable in claim language where there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the list of potential alternatives can vary and ambiguity arises, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is proper; exam decisions include Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu. Examiner must analyze whether 'optionally' creates confusion about alternatives covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations are not inherently ambiguous or uncertain so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely (even if negatively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older courts criticized negative limitations, but more recent cases find them definite when boundaries are clear (e.g., In re Wakefield, In re Barr). Any negative limitation or exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure; if alternative elements are positively recited in the specification they may be explicitly excluded in the claims (In re Johnson). A negative limitation without basis in the original disclosure should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (written description). Lack of literal basis in the specification for a negative limitation may not by itself be sufficient to establish a prima facie lack of descriptive support (Ex parte Parks). See MPEP § 2163–§ 2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old combination rejection disfavored
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'old combination'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the 1952 Patent Act, the old-combination principle (Lincoln Engineering) is no longer a valid basis for rejection; claims should be considered proper if they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. See cases including In re Bernhart, Ex parte Barber, and Radio Steel and Mfg. Co. v. MTD Products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation is non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection for 'aggregation' is non‑statutory (In re Gustafson, In re Collier). If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements, other statutes or MPEP § 2172.01 may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when they contain such long recitations or unimportant details that the scope of the claimed invention is rendered indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject when long recitations prevent determination of the metes and bounds of claimed subject matter (i.e., render claim indefinite). Use rejection sparingly and only where indefiniteness results from prolixity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity / undue multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented provided they differ substantially from each other and are not unduly multiplied (37 CFR 1.75).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicant presents an unreasonable number of repetitious claims that confuse rather than clarify, an undue multiplicity rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate. Examiners should apply the rule of reason and be judicious; undue multiplicity rejections should be rare. If rejection is appropriate, examiner should contact applicant (telephone) to request selection of specified number of claims for examination; follow procedures to preserve applicant's right to Board review. See case law (In re Chandler, In re Flint) and Ex parte Whitelaw doctrine for restriction of duplicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule that 'double inclusion' is improper in a claim; the governing consideration is the reasonable construction of claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts of each case must be evaluated to determine whether multiple inclusion of one or more elements gives rise to indefiniteness. A compound embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not automatically create uncertainty; however, device claims that can be read to include the same element twice may be indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen). Older cases should be applied with care (Ex parte White, Ex parte Clark, In re Kelly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim (a product claim that defines the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made) is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A device, apparatus, manufacture, or composition claim may reference the process in which it is intended to be used without being objectionable under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, provided it is clear the claim is directed to the product and not the process. Applicants may present claims of varying scope even when necessary to describe the claimed product in product-by-process terms (cases: In re Luck, In re Pilkington, In re Steppan, Ex parte Pantzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and process in same claim (improper)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim which claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System claims that recite actions of users or method steps can create confusion as to when infringement occurs and have been held indefinite (In re Katz Interactive Call Processing Patent Litigation; IPXL v. Amazon; Ex parte Lyell). Examiners should reject such claims as indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Use" claims (process without steps) are problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps involved in the process raise an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting mere use (e.g., 'A process for using monoclonal antibodies...') have been held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Some authorities suggest 35 U.S.C. 101 may be more appropriate in certain cases. Recommended practice: reject 'use' claims under alternative grounds based on 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112. However, claims that clearly recite a step of 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite in some cases (Ex parte Porter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claims should be rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Omnibus claims (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') are indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language (Ex parte Fressola). Use Form Paragraph 7.35 for rejection; see MPEP § 706.03(d) and § 1302.04(b) for examiner amendment/cancellation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to figures or tables in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, claims are to be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity doctrine', not for applicant convenience. Use only where no practical way to define invention in words and where incorporation is more concise than duplicating drawing or table. Reference characters corresponding to elements in detailed description/drawings may be used with recitation of same element(s) in claims. See Ex parte Fressola and MPEP § 608.01(m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical formula claims not indefinite absent error
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions often use formulas; these structures should not be considered indefinite or speculative in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of corroborating spectroscopic or other data cannot be the basis for finding the structure indefinite (Ex parte Morton, Ex parte Sobin). A claim is not indefinite merely because a structure is not fully presented (In re Fisher). Compounds may be claimed by an adequate name, a combination of physical/chemical characteristics, or by the process by which made (Ex parte Brian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks/trade names in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, but must be carefully analyzed to determine how the mark/name is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trademark identifies a source of goods, not the goods themselves; using a trademark/trade name to identify or describe a particular material/product renders the claim indefinite and is improper (Ex parte Simpson). If a trademark appears but is not intended as a limitation, examiner should ask whether its presence causes confusion about claim scope; if so, reject under 112, second paragraph. See MPEP § 608.01(v) and Appendix I for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere function of a machine (process claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process or method claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, solely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the process claim is otherwise patentable, it should not be rejected merely because disclosed apparatus will inherently carry out the recited steps (In re Tarczy-Hornoch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Compact Prosecution — interpret claim and apply art with explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under compact prosecution, the examiner should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action to avoid unnecessary delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim term or phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and also make rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 as they apply based on the examiner's interpretation of the claim. The examiner must state on the record how the claim term is being interpreted relative to prior art to avoid piecemeal examination (see 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1); MPEP § 706; § 707.07(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art rejection strategy for indefinite claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches for handling prior art rejections when claims are considered indefinite: (1) where uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders claim unpatentable, enter both an indefiniteness rejection and a prior-art rejection based on the interpretation; (2) where great confusion exists, do not base a rejection on prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First approach is generally recommended to avoid piecemeal examination and to give applicant appreciation for relevant prior art; when making prior-art rejections based on an interpretation, the examiner must state how the claim is being interpreted. If the claim is highly ambiguous such that meaningful prior-art comparison would require speculation, prior-art rejection should be avoided (In re Steele). See Ex parte Ionescu for example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C.112 first and second paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of the first and second paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 112 are separate and distinct: lack of commensurate enabling disclosure is a 112 first-paragraph issue (written description/enablement), whereas indefiniteness is a 112 second-paragraph issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification disclosure/enabling disclosure is not commensurate in scope with the claim, the claim should be rejected under 112, first paragraph (e.g., In re Borkowski). If the specification discloses a feature as essential, failure to recite it in the claim may be a 112 first-paragraph problem (In re Mayhew). Amending a claim to include matter not described in the application as filed may warrant a 112 first-paragraph rejection (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi). Examiners should distinguish between lack of descriptive support/enablement and indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying 35 U.S.C.112 sixth paragraph (means/step-plus-function) limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for examination of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph 'means or step plus function' limitations: such limitations must be interpreted consistent with the written description of the invention and Donaldson requires giving effect to corresponding structure disclosed in the specification when construing means-plus-function language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Donaldson, the PTO may not disregard structure disclosed in the specification when construing means-plus-function language; examiners must apply 112, sixth paragraph where appropriate while giving claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. See In re Donaldson, TriMed v. Stryker, Altiris v. Symantec, and related Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑prong test for invoking 112 sixth paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term (a term simply substituting for 'means for'); (B) the phrase is modified by functional language; and (C) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limitation is presumed to invoke 112 sixth paragraph when it explicitly uses 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language; that presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function (TriMed). Conversely, absence of the phrase 'means for' triggers a rebuttable presumption that 112 sixth paragraph does not apply (Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media). The presumption is strong and not readily overcome (Lighting World, Inventio). Non-structural 'nonce' words may be treated as equivalents of 'means for' if they are not recognized names of structure (Lighting World). Examiners should analyze whether the claim recites sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment.
